14010: A runaway is something or someone that has broken free from control and is now moving, acting, or existing outside the bounds of where it should be — often in a way that is hard or impossible to stop.
The Most Common Use: A Person

The most frequent meaning of runaway as a noun is a person — almost always a child or teenager — who has secretly left home without permission and without telling anyone where they are going.

This person hasn't just gone for a walk. They've made a deliberate choice to leave, usually because something at home has become unbearable — abuse, conflict, extreme unhappiness, or fear. They are now living on their own, without their family's knowledge or approval.

"The police found the runaway hiding in an abandoned building."

"The shelter downtown takes in runaways and helps connect them with social workers."

Notice that the word itself carries a quiet weight. When you hear "a runaway," you instinctively sense vulnerability and urgency. It is not a neutral word. It suggests someone in trouble, someone escaping from something painful, and often someone who is now in danger.

Historically, the word was also used for enslaved people who escaped to freedom — people who literally ran away from captivity. This older usage still lives in historical writing.
A Runaway Can Also Be an Animal

The second common use of runaway as a noun refers to an animal — typically a horse — that has broken free from its handler and is running out of control.

"The runaway galloped straight through the marketplace before anyone could stop it."

A horse is powerful. When one breaks loose and bolts, no one can simply grab it and make it stop. That sense of uncontrollable momentum is exactly what the word captures.
A Runaway Can Also Be a Vehicle

A runaway can also refer to a vehicle — a truck, a train, a cart — that is moving without anyone controlling it, usually because the brakes have failed or no one is at the wheel.

"Emergency crews worked to slow the runaway before it reached the crowded station."

This is the same underlying idea: something that was supposed to be under control has broken free and is now going wherever momentum takes it.
What All These Meanings Have in Common

No matter whether the runaway is a teenager, a horse, or a truck — the word always signals three things:

  1. Escape — it has left where it was supposed to be.
  2. Loss of control — no one is currently steering or stopping it.
  3. Urgency — the situation demands immediate attention.

This is what makes runaway such a vivid word. It doesn't just describe movement. It describes movement that has gone rogue.

As a noun, it follows normal rules:

  • One person: a runaway
  • Many people: runaways

"The city's shelters were overwhelmed by the number of runaways seeking help."

There is a difference between someone who runs away (the action) and someone who is a runaway (the identity or label).

  • "She ran away from home last Thursday." → This describes what she did.
  • "She is a runaway." → This describes who she now is — someone living outside the home, unaccounted for.

The noun runaway is the label given to someone once running away has become their situation, not just a momentary act.

A runaway (noun) is a person (especially a young person who has fled home), an animal, or a vehicle that has escaped from control and is now moving or existing in an uncontrolled, unsanctioned way — often urgently and dangerously. The word always carries the idea of something that broke free and cannot easily be brought back.
14011:
A rundown is a structured summary or overview of something — a clear, organized account of the main points, details, or facts about a topic, situation, or event.

Think of it this way: imagine you missed a long, two-hour meeting at work. You don't have time to read the full 20-page report of what happened. So you ask a colleague, "Can you give me a rundown of the meeting?" They then tell you the key things that were discussed — briefly, clearly, and in an organized way. That summary they give you? That is a rundown.

A rundown is not just any summary. It has a few important qualities baked into it:

  • It is organized. A rundown goes through things in a logical order — often point by point, or item by item. It doesn't jump around randomly.
  • It covers the essential information. It includes what you need to know, without burying you in unnecessary detail.
  • It is relatively brief relative to the full subject. A rundown is not an exhaustive deep dive — it's a smart, efficient overview.

So the word sits comfortably between a vague mention (too little) and an overwhelming full report (too much). A rundown is the sweet spot — enough to clearly understand something.

While the core idea stays the same, "rundown" gets used in two slightly different ways depending on context:

1. A quick overview (the lighter version)
Here, a rundown is a fast, high-level summary — just the highlights. You use this when you want the big picture fast.

"Before the game starts, the commentator gave a rundown of each player on the team."

"Let me give you a quick rundown of today's schedule."

2. A thorough breakdown (the more detailed version)
Here, a rundown is a more complete, systematic account that goes through everything carefully, piece by piece. It's still organized and efficient, but more comprehensive.

"The accountant gave us a rundown of all the expenses for the year."

"She prepared a detailed rundown of every step in the process."

The difference between these two is mostly signaled by the adjective placed before it — quick rundown vs. detailed rundown vs. full rundown. Without any adjective, context usually makes the intended depth clear.

In baseball, a rundown has a very specific, technical meaning. It refers to a play where a baserunner gets caught between two bases, and the fielders on both sides chase the runner back and forth, trying to tag them out before they can safely reach either base. It's essentially a trap. This play is also sometimes called a "pickle" in casual baseball talk, but rundown is the standard term.

This meaning is entirely separate from the "summary" meaning. Context (a sports conversation vs. a general conversation) will always make it clear which one is intended.

In everyday language, you will almost always see "rundown" used with a small set of very natural verb and adjective pairings. Getting familiar with these will help you use and recognize the word naturally:

Common verbs used with "rundown":

  • give a rundown
  • get a rundown
  • provide a rundown
  • need a rundown
  • do a rundown

Common adjectives used before "rundown":

  • a quick rundown
  • a brief rundown
  • a full rundown
  • a complete rundown
  • a detailed rundown
What Makes "Rundown" Different from Similar Words?

You might wonder how "rundown" differs from words like summary, overview, or recap. Here's the distinction:

  • A summary is a general word — it just means a shortened version of something.
  • An overview tends to be more formal and high-level, like a bird's-eye view.
  • A recap usually refers specifically to repeating what already happened — it looks backward.
  • A rundown implies going through things systematically — it feels more like a structured list or briefing being delivered to you. It has an active, organized, almost "item-by-item" feel to it.

If someone says "Let me give you a rundown," you instinctively expect them to go through the points in a clear, organized sequence — not just give you a vague description.
A Few More Examples in Real Life

• "Before the surgery, the doctor gave me a rundown of all the risks involved."
  • "The coach gave the team a full rundown of the opponent's strategy."
  • "Can someone give me a rundown of what I missed while I was on vacation?"
  • "The guide provided a rundown of the museum's most important exhibits."
  • "The financial report included a rundown of every department's spending."

The noun rundown means a clear, organized summary or breakdown of information — covering the key facts or details of something in an efficient and structured way. It can be brief or detailed depending on context. Outside of a baseball setting, if someone asks for "a rundown," they want you to walk them through the important points in an organized, easy-to-follow way.
14012: A rune is a single character — a letter — from an ancient writing system used by Germanic and Norse peoples of Northern and Western Europe, primarily from around the 2nd century CE onward. These characters together formed what are called runic alphabets, the most well-known of which is the Elder Futhark (a set of 24 characters).

Runes look nothing like the letters you are reading right now. They are angular — built almost entirely from straight lines and sharp diagonal strokes, with very few curves. This is not accidental. Runes were almost never written on paper or parchment. Instead, they were carved — into stone, wood, bone, metal, or antler. When you are cutting into a hard surface with a blade or chisel, curves are difficult and impractical. Straight lines are not. So the shapes of runes evolved to suit carving. This is why a runic inscription on a stone looks so different from, say, written Latin.
Runes as letters with names and meanings

This is where runes differ from ordinary letters in a fascinating way. Each rune was not just a sound or a letter — it also had its own name and its own meaning. For example, one rune was called Fehu, and it represented the "F" sound, but Fehu also meant "cattle" or "wealth." Another rune, Tiwaz, represented the sound "T" and was named after Tyr, a Norse god associated with justice and war.

So when someone in ancient times carved a rune, they were not simply spelling out a word the way you might type a letter. They were also invoking the symbolic weight of that rune's meaning. This dual nature — letter and symbol — is central to understanding what a rune is.

This is impossible to separate from the concept of a rune, because historically the two were inseparable.

Ancient Germanic and Norse peoples believed that runes were not merely invented by humans — they were considered sacred, discovered knowledge, gifts of cosmic power. Runes were thought to carry real, active power. Carving a rune into an object was not just labeling it; it was believed to imbue that object with something — protection, strength, a curse, a blessing.

This meant runes were used in rituals, in spells, inscribed on weapons to make them more powerful in battle, on amulets to protect the wearer, on grave markers to honor and perhaps guard the dead. They were written on objects to invoke luck, healing, or harm.

As a result, the word rune came to carry a second, broader meaning: a mysterious or magical symbol — any mark, character, or sign believed to hold hidden power. This usage is not purely metaphorical; it reflects how deeply magic and writing were intertwined in these cultures.

By extension, rune stones are small, flat stones (or tiles made of wood, clay, or other materials) each inscribed with a single runic character. A set typically contains all the characters of a runic alphabet.

These are used for divination — a practice of seeking guidance, insight, or answers about the future or present circumstances. The person consulting the runes might draw one or several stones at random, then interpret the meaning of whichever rune(s) appeared. Each rune, with its symbolic meaning, is read as a kind of message or indicator.

Rune stones in this sense are not about ancient writing at all — they are a tool for seeking hidden knowledge. This practice connects back to the idea of runes as magical and meaningful beyond mere letters.
How the word is used today

Today, the word rune is used in a few overlapping ways:

  1. In historical and linguistic contexts, a rune is simply one character from a runic alphabet. Scholars, historians, and linguists use it this way.
  2. In spiritual and New Age contexts, runes (usually rune stones) are used for divination and self-reflection, drawing on the old symbolic meanings of each character.
  3. In fantasy, literature, games, and popular culture, the word rune has been adopted very broadly to mean any magical symbol or inscription — often one that grants power, activates a spell, or holds supernatural energy. Video games, novels, and films use it this way constantly. Here, a "rune" might not resemble historical runic writing at all — it's simply a mark with mystical force.
  4. Poetically or figuratively, a rune can refer to any mysterious, arcane, or deeply meaningful mark or inscription — something that seems to hold a secret or hidden significance.

A rune is, at its most precise, a single character from an ancient Germanic or Norse writing system — but one where every character also carried a name, a symbolic meaning, and was believed to hold real power. That belief in power is what stretched the word outward: today it means not just those ancient letters, but any symbol considered mysterious, magical, or charged with hidden significance. When you see the word rune — in a history book, a fantasy novel, or a spiritual text — it always carries this combination: the idea of a mark that means something beyond its surface appearance, whether that's a sound, a concept, a force, or a secret.
14013:
A rung is one of the horizontal bars on a ladder — the individual steps you place your feet on when climbing up or down.

Picture a typical ladder leaning against a wall. It has two long vertical rails running up the sides. Connecting those two rails, from top to bottom, are a series of short horizontal bars spaced evenly apart. Each one of those bars is a rung. Together, they give you a surface to step on as you climb.

So if a ladder has ten steps, it has ten rungs. The word refers to a single one of those steps.

The word "rung" isn't limited to ladders. It also refers to the horizontal bars connecting the legs of a chair — the small crossbars near the bottom that brace the legs together and keep the chair sturdy. These are also called rungs. You might hear someone say, "The cat scratched the rungs of the chair."

This is where the word becomes truly powerful and frequently used.

Because a ladder has levels — with the bottom rung being the lowest and the top rung being the highest — people use "rung" as a metaphor to describe a level or position within any system, hierarchy, or scale.

Think of society, a company, or a career as an invisible ladder. Every step up that ladder is a rung.

Examples:

  • "She started at the bottom rung of the company and worked her way up to manager."
    → She started at the lowest level and rose higher.
  • "Being born into a wealthy family placed him on a higher rung of society."
    → He occupied a higher position or status in society.
  • "He's still on the lowest rung of his career."
    → He's still a beginner, at the starting level.
  • "Moving to a senior role was a big step up the ladder — she had climbed another rung."
    → She advanced one level higher.

The key idea here is levels — like steps you can move up or down. A rung is one specific level within that progression.

The plural of rung is simply rungs.

  • "Be careful — two of the ladder's rungs are broken."
  • "He has climbed many rungs to get where he is today."

ContextWhat "rung" means
  • On a ladder or chair: a single horizontal bar or crosspiece.
  • In life, society, or work: a single level or step in a system of ranks or positions.

The connecting thread between both meanings is the same: a rung is always one distinct step or level within something that has multiple levels stacked above and below it. Whether it's a physical ladder you climb with your feet, or an imaginary one representing your career or social status, a rung is always one specific position on that scale.
14014: "Runic" means of, relating to, or written in runes. It describes anything connected to runes — the ancient carved letters of Northern European peoples. To truly understand "runic," you need to understand what runes are, so let's start there.

Runes are the characters of an ancient alphabet (actually a family of related alphabets) used by Germanic peoples — particularly the Vikings, Anglo-Saxons, and other Norse peoples — roughly from 200 AD onward, with some forms surviving even into the 1600s in Scandinavia.

What makes runes visually distinctive is that they look nothing like the smooth, curved letters you're reading right now. Runes are angular and geometric — think sharp strokes and straight lines with no curves. This is because they were designed to be carved into hard surfaces: stone, wood, bone, and metal. Carving curves into rock is difficult; straight lines are not. So the alphabet was shaped by its method of writing.

Each individual character in a runic alphabet is called a rune. The most famous runic alphabet is called the Elder Futhark, which has 24 such characters.
"Runic" carries two related but distinct meanings, and both are in active use today.

In its direct sense, "runic" simply means of or relating to actual historical runes. This is the technical use — used by historians, archaeologists, and linguists.

  • A runic inscription is text carved or written in runes.
  • A runic alphabet is any alphabet made of runic characters.
  • A runic stone (also called a runestone) is a stone bearing runic carving.
  • Runic script refers to runes treated as a writing system.

Example: "Runic inscriptions have been found across Scandinavia, the British Isles, and parts of Eastern Europe."
2. The figurative meaning: mysterious and cryptic

Here is where the word becomes richer. Runes were never just an alphabet. In the ancient world, they were believed to carry magical power. Warriors had runes carved onto their weapons to make them deadlier. People wore runic amulets for protection. Runes were connected to Odin, the Norse god of wisdom and war, who was said to have discovered them through great suffering. Because of this deep, historical association with secrecy, magic, and hidden knowledge, "runic" came to mean something beyond the alphabet itself: mysterious, cryptic, hard to read or interpret, and carrying a sense of hidden power.

When a writer uses "runic" figuratively, they mean something that:

  • Is deliberately obscure or hard to understand
  • Hints at hidden meaning beneath the surface
  • Carries an air of ancient mystery or secret knowledge

Examples:

  • "He gave a runic smile." — His smile seemed to conceal some secret; it was unreadable.
  • "Her instructions were runic." — Her instructions were so cryptic and unclear that no one could make sense of them.
  • "The old prophet spoke in runic riddles." — He spoke in deliberately obscure, mysterious language.

This figurative use appears often in literature, journalism, and academic writing.

Whether used literally or figuratively, "runic" almost always brings a particular atmosphere with it. It evokes:

  • Antiquity — something from a deep, distant past
  • Mystery — something not easily read or understood, like a code
  • Hidden power — the sense that this thing carries meaning beyond what is visible
  • The Norse world — carved stones in cold, windswept landscapes; ancient wisdom; old gods

This is precisely why "runic" is so widely used in fantasy literature and games. When a fantasy author writes about "runic markings" or a "runic blade," they are not necessarily referring to actual historical Norse runes. They are borrowing the atmosphere the word carries — the feeling of ancient, magical, encoded power. The word does heavy lifting just by being there.

It helps to know how "runic" sits alongside words that seem similar:

  • Cryptic means difficult to understand, but it has no historical or mystical weight — a cryptic crossword clue is just confusing.
  • Arcane means known only to a few; secretive or esoteric. It's closer to "runic" in feeling, but "arcane" suggests restricted knowledge, while "runic" suggests visually encoded or symbolically charged mystery.
  • Mystical suggests a connection to spiritual or supernatural forces, without the specific visual/written quality that "runic" carries.
  • Ancient just means old.

"Runic" is unique because it fuses the idea of a visual written symbol with mystery and ancient power. It is specific in a way the others are not.

• In history and archaeology: "The runestone bears a runic inscription dating to the 9th century."
  • In linguistics: "Old Norse was sometimes recorded in runic script."
  • In literature and fiction: "The cave walls were covered in glowing runic symbols, each one humming faintly with energy."
  • In metaphorical use: "He nodded with a runic expression, as though he alone understood what was coming."

"Runic" primarily means relating to runes — the angular, carved letters of ancient Germanic peoples, deeply associated with the Vikings and Norse culture. By natural extension, it also means mysterious, cryptic, or symbolically charged, because runes were historically tied to magic, hidden wisdom, and divine power. Whenever you encounter "runic," ask one question: is the writer referring to actual historical runes, or are they using the word to evoke a feeling of ancient mystery and encoded meaning? Both uses are correct, both are common, and once you know the connection between the two, the word will feel completely clear in any context.
14015:
A runnel is a very small, narrow stream of flowing water. Think of it as one step above a mere trickle — water that is actually moving along a defined little path, but is too tiny and thin to be called a stream or a brook.

If a river is a highway for water, and a stream is a side road, then a runnel is a tiny footpath — barely wide enough, barely deep enough, but water is moving through it with clear direction.

Imagine it is raining heavily. The water hits the ground and begins to flow downhill. As it does, it carves out small, thin channels along the surface of the mud or soil. Those thin little channels of moving water? Each one is a runnel.

Or picture a hillside after a storm. You look down at the slope and see dozens of tiny little rivers — each only a few centimetres wide — threading their way down through the grass and earth. Those are runnels.

Or think of a cobblestone street after heavy rain. Water gathers and flows in a thin, narrow line along the edge of the road, hugging the kerb. That thin moving line of water is also a runnel.

The word carries two senses that are deeply connected to each other:

1. The water itself — a runnel is the actual small stream, the thin flow of water moving from one place to another. In this sense, the runnel is the water.

2. The channel it flows through — a runnel can also refer to the narrow little groove or channel in the ground through which water flows. In this sense, the runnel is the path, the physical hollow or cut in the earth that guides the water.

In practice, these two senses blend together almost seamlessly. When someone says "a runnel ran down the hillside," you picture both the channel and the water in it as one single thing. This is perfectly natural and how the word is normally used.
How Small Is a Runnel, Exactly?

This is worth pinning down. A runnel is:

  • Smaller than a stream. A stream has some substance to it — you might step across a stream carefully. A runnel you barely even notice underfoot.
  • Smaller than a brook. A brook is a cheerful, bubbling small waterway. A runnel is much quieter and thinner than that.
  • Similar to a rivulet. A rivulet is the closest synonym — both words describe a very small, thin flow of water. A runnel, however, often implies something slightly more temporary or surface-level, like rain-fed trickles, while "rivulet" can sound slightly more established. But this difference is subtle, and in most real-world usage the two words are interchangeable.
  • Bigger than a mere drip or trickle. A trickle is almost reluctant — just a few drops moving slowly. A runnel has just enough water to form a proper, moving little flow with a visible path.

Think of runnels as the smallest unit of something you would still confidently call a "stream."
Where You'll Encounter Runnels in Real Life

Runnels appear in very specific, recognisable situations:

  • After rain: This is the most common setting. Rain falls, collects, and runs downhill in thin channels across fields, roads, footpaths, and slopes. These are runnels.
  • On a beach: When a wave washes up on sand and then retreats, it often carves small channels in the sand as the water drains back toward the sea. Those are runnels.
  • On a windowpane: Some people use "runnel" loosely to describe the thin lines of water running down a wet glass surface, though this is a more poetic or extended use.
  • In mountains and moorlands: Rocky hillsides and moorlands are full of runnels — thin streams of water finding their way between rocks and through heather after rainfall.
  • In gutters and pavements: A thin stream of water running along the edge of a road or a drainage channel can be called a runnel.

Seeing a word used in sentences makes its meaning truly stick:

  • After the storm, runnels of water zigzagged down the muddy path.
  • She watched a small runnel carve its way through the sand as the tide pulled back.
  • The hillside was streaked with runnels, each one catching the grey light of the sky.
  • A thin runnel of melted snow trickled along the edge of the road.
  • He knelt down and touched the runnel with his finger — barely a centimetre wide, but cold and quick.

Notice how in each of these sentences, the runnel is small, moving, and water-based. It always carries those three qualities.
The Emotional and Descriptive Weight of the Word

"Runnel" is not a word you'll hear in everyday conversation. It belongs mostly to written language — especially descriptive writing, nature writing, poetry, and literary fiction. Writers reach for it when they want to describe small water flows with precision and a certain quiet beauty. It is a gentle, unassuming word that perfectly fits its subject: small, unobtrusive, quietly purposeful flows of water.

When you read the word "runnel" in a book, the author is almost always trying to paint a careful, close-up picture of a landscape — drawing your eye to something small and delicate that you might otherwise overlook.

If you had to compress everything above into a single sentence to remember forever:

A runnel is a very small, narrow stream of flowing water — or the thin channel it flows through — typically formed by rain on a slope, a hillside, a beach, or a road.

That is the word, completely and accurately understood.
14016: At the heart of nearly every adjective use of "running" is one simple image: something that keeps going without stopping. Like a river that never pauses, something "running" is continuous, uninterrupted, or in constant motion. Keep this image in mind — it will make every meaning below feel intuitive.

1. Continuing over time, without a break

This is the most common use. When "running" describes something, it means that thing is ongoing — not a one-time event, but something that persists, recurs, or keeps happening.

  • A running battle — a conflict or disagreement that never fully ends; it keeps flaring up again and again. Politicians often have a running battle over tax policy for years.
  • A running joke — a joke that gets repeated among a group of people over a long period. Everyone in the friend group laughs at it every time it comes up, because it has a history.
  • A running commentary — a continuous, real-time description of something as it happens. A cricket commentator giving a ball-by-ball description of a match is giving a running commentary.
  • A running debate — a discussion or argument that people keep returning to without ever fully settling it.
  • A running total — a total figure that you keep updating every time new numbers come in. If you're tracking daily sales and you add each new sale to the previous sum throughout the day, you're keeping a running total.
  • Running costs (also called running expenses) — the regular, ongoing costs of keeping something in operation: electricity, salaries, maintenance. These are different from a one-time purchase cost. A business owner worries about running costs every single month.

The common thread: none of these things happen once and finish. They keep going.

2. One after another, with no gap in between (consecutively)

Here, "running" describes an unbroken sequence — things happening back to back, with no interruption in between.

This is special because, in this meaning, "running" almost always comes after the noun or number it describes, not before it.

  • "It rained for ten days running." — Ten consecutive days. No dry day in between.
  • "She won the championship three years running." — She won in year one, year two, and year three, without anyone else winning in between.
  • "He called me five times running." — Five calls, one after another.

Notice: you would say "five times running," not "five running times." The word sits at the end in this use. This is an important pattern to remember.

3. Flowing continuously (water or liquid)

When "running" describes water, it means water that is actively flowing — not sitting still in a tank or pool.

  • Running water — water that flows through pipes and comes out when you open a tap. This is considered a basic modern necessity. Many villages in developing areas lack running water and have to fetch it from wells or rivers.
  • A running stream — a stream that is currently flowing (as opposed to one that has dried up).
  • A running tap — a tap that has been left open and is actively releasing water.

4. Discharging fluid continuously (wounds, infections, the nose)

When a sore, wound, or nose is "running," it means it is producing and releasing liquid without stopping.

  • A running sore — a wound or infected area that keeps oozing or weeping fluid. It never dries and heals; it just keeps producing fluid. This phrase is also used figuratively: a "running sore" can mean a long-standing problem that causes ongoing pain and never gets resolved — like a territory dispute between two countries that has caused conflict for generations.
  • A running nose — you'll more often hear "runny nose," but "running nose" describes the same thing: a nose that keeps dripping mucus.

5. Currently operating or switched on (machines and engines)

"Running" can describe a machine or engine that is actively on and working at this moment.

  • "Don't reach into a running machine." — A machine that is currently in operation.
  • "She left the engine running." — The engine was left switched on.
  • "A running generator can be dangerous indoors." — A generator that is currently on and producing power.

6. Designed for or used in the sport of running

When placed before certain nouns, "running" describes things that exist for the purpose of the sport or activity of running.

  • Running shoes — shoes specifically designed for running.
  • Running track — a track where people run races.
  • Running gear — the clothing and equipment a runner uses.
  • Running club — a club whose members come together to run.

A small note: in this use, "running" is describing purpose ("made for running") rather than the idea of continuity. It's a slightly different flavour, but it's still used to modify a noun just like any adjective.

A few specific phrases built with "running" as an adjective come up so often that they deserve their own mention:

Running order — the sequence in which things are scheduled to happen. At a music festival, the running order tells you which band performs when, and in what sequence.

Running mate — in politics, the person who is chosen to run alongside a main candidate, usually for a lower office. When a party picks a presidential candidate, that candidate then picks a running mate to be the vice-presidential candidate. They run as a pair.

Running head (or running header) — in books, documents, or magazines, a line of text that appears at the top of every page, usually showing the book title or the chapter name. It "runs" across all the pages.

A running start — beginning something with momentum already built up. If you take a running start at a problem, you're not starting from zero; you've already done some preparation. Used both literally (running and jumping) and figuratively.
The One Thread That Ties It All Together

If you want a single anchor for your memory: "running" as an adjective almost always means something is in continuous, uninterrupted motion or activity — it doesn't stop, it keeps going.

Water keeps flowing → running water.
A fight keeps recurring → a running battle.
Days keep coming one after another → three days running.
A machine keeps operating → a running engine.
A wound keeps weeping → a running sore.

The image of a river — always moving, never pooling, never pausing — is the best mental picture you can carry for this word.
14017: Before diving into the different meanings, here's the unifying idea that runs through all of them: runoff is what happens when a system reaches its limit and the excess spills over or flows away. Keep this in mind — it makes every meaning feel intuitive.
Meaning 1: Water That Flows Over Land (The Primary Meaning)

This is the most widely used meaning, especially in science, environment, and everyday conversation.

When rain falls or snow melts, the earth can only absorb so much water. Think of the soil like a sponge — a sponge can hold a certain amount of liquid, but once it's full, any extra liquid just runs right off it. The water that the ground cannot soak in starts flowing across the surface — over roads, fields, rooftops, hillsides, and parking lots — until it eventually reaches a stream, river, lake, or the ocean.

That excess water flowing across the surface of the land is called runoff.

Example: After a heavy storm, you can literally see runoff — the water streaming across the road, rushing down gutters, or flowing through ditches.

Why Runoff Matters

Understanding runoff is not just a geography lesson — it has real consequences:

Flooding. When there is too much runoff and water bodies cannot absorb it fast enough, the excess water overflows onto land. Cities pave over natural soil, which means rain has fewer places to soak in, so urban areas often experience heavy runoff and are more flood-prone.

Pollution. As runoff flows across the land, it picks up whatever it passes over — fertilizers from farms, oil and grease from roads, pesticides from gardens, animal waste, industrial chemicals. It carries all of this into rivers and lakes. This is why you'll often hear the phrases:

  • Agricultural runoff — water carrying fertilizers and pesticides from farmland into rivers, often causing excessive algae growth in lakes (called eutrophication).
  • Urban runoff — water flowing off city roads and rooftops, carrying pollutants into local waterways.
  • Stormwater runoff — a broader term for all the water generated by rain events that flows off surfaces rather than soaking in.

Erosion. Runoff physically moves soil particles as it flows. Over time, this strips away the top layer of soil (the most fertile layer), damages hillsides, and silts up rivers.

Drought and water supply. Ironically, too much runoff can contribute to drought. If water rushes away as runoff instead of soaking into the ground, it doesn't replenish groundwater reserves, which are what wells and springs depend on.

The Water Cycle Connection

Runoff is a key part of the water cycle. Rain falls → some evaporates, some soaks into the ground, and the rest becomes runoff → runoff flows into rivers and oceans → water evaporates from those bodies → it forms clouds → it rains again.

The second major meaning is completely different in subject but follows the same logic: what happens when no clear outcome is reached in the first attempt.

A runoff (also called a runoff election) is a second round of voting held because the first election did not produce a winner who meets the required threshold — usually an outright majority (more than 50% of the votes).

Here's why it happens:

Imagine an election with three candidates:

  • Candidate A gets 40% of the votes
  • Candidate B gets 35% of the votes
  • Candidate C gets 25% of the votes

Candidate A won the most votes, but not a majority — more than half of voters preferred someone else. Many electoral systems require a winner to have majority support, not just more votes than the others. So the election is unresolved after the first round.

A runoff is then held between the top two finishers (A and B in this case). Voters now choose between just those two candidates, so one of them must get a majority. The runoff produces a clear, decisive winner.

Example sentences:

  • "No candidate crossed the 50% threshold, so the race will go to a runoff next month."
  • "The two candidates who advanced to the runoff spent weeks campaigning intensively."

Runoff elections are common in many countries, U.S. Senate and gubernatorial races in some states (notably Georgia), and local elections. The specific rules vary — some systems require exactly 50%+1 to avoid a runoff; others set a different threshold.
Meaning 3: Overflow or Leftover in a Process (Specialized/Technical)

In industrial, manufacturing, and financial contexts, runoff can refer to the leftover, overflow, or gradual tail-end of a process — what remains after the main activity is complete.

  • In manufacturing, runoff can describe excess material (like molten metal or paint) that overflows or drips away during production.
  • In finance and insurance, a "runoff" refers to a situation where a company stops taking on new business but continues managing its existing obligations until they are all settled — like a gradual winding-down. An insurance company in runoff, for instance, is still paying out old claims but not issuing new policies.
  • More generally, "runoff" can describe any gradual diminishment — the slow expiration of a portfolio, contracts, or liabilities over time.

This usage is technical and context-specific. You'll mostly encounter it in finance, insurance, and industrial settings.

The word "runoff" always carries the idea of excess flowing away, spilling over, or what happens after the main capacity is used up.

ContextWhat "runs off"
Water & environmentRain that the ground can't absorb
ElectionsVotes that didn't decide a winner in round one
Finance/industryObligations or material that remain after the main process ends

If you want to remember this word in its most important sense: Runoff is what flows away when something can't hold any more. Water runs off land. Votes "run over" into a second election. Obligations run off slowly at the tail end of a business.

That's runoff — completely and accurately explained.

A rupture is a sudden, forceful break — the moment something that was whole, sealed, or connected tears apart or bursts open, often under pressure.

Think of a water balloon that has been filled beyond its limit and suddenly pops. That moment of breaking — that violent splitting — is a rupture. Or imagine a pipe underground that has been carrying water for decades. One day, the pressure becomes too much, and the pipe cracks open, sending water gushing out. That, too, is a rupture.

The word carries a sense of force and suddenness. It is not a slow, gentle separation. It is a break that happens abruptly — and often with serious consequences.

The word lives comfortably in two worlds: the physical and the abstract.

1. Physical Rupture

This is the most literal sense — something material actually breaks open or bursts.

Examples:

  • A gas pipe develops a rupture, causing a dangerous leak.
  • The dam suffered a rupture after weeks of heavy rain.
  • There was a rupture in the fuel tank of the aircraft.

Here, a rupture almost always implies:

  • Something was intact and sealed before (a pipe, a membrane, a container).
  • Something forced it open — pressure, stress, or trauma.
  • The result is usually leakage, damage, or danger.

2. Medical Rupture

Medicine uses this word very specifically. In the human body, organs, tissues, blood vessels, and membranes can rupture. This means they tear or burst, usually with serious medical consequences.

Common examples:

  • A ruptured appendix — the appendix swells with infection and eventually bursts, which is a life-threatening emergency.
  • A ruptured blood vessel — a vessel in the body tears open, causing internal bleeding.
  • A ruptured eardrum — the thin membrane inside your ear is torn, usually by a loud blast, pressure change, or an infection.
  • A hernia rupture — a weak spot in the abdominal wall tears further.
  • A ruptured tendon — a tendon (the tissue connecting your muscle to your bone) snaps.

In medicine, a rupture is almost always serious — it signals that something the body depends on to stay closed and intact has given way.

3. Abstract Rupture (Relationships, Agreements, and Social Bonds)

This is perhaps the most interesting use. A rupture doesn't have to involve anything physical at all. It can describe the sudden breaking of a relationship, an agreement, a peace, or a sense of unity between people, groups, or nations.

Just as a pipe ruptures under too much pressure, a relationship can rupture when stress, conflict, or betrayal becomes too great.

Examples:

  • A bitter argument caused a rupture in their friendship that never fully healed.
  • The scandal led to a rupture in diplomatic relations between the two countries.
  • The disagreement over money created a rupture within the family.
  • The leaked document caused a rupture in the peace talks.

In this sense, a rupture means:

  • A relationship or bond that previously held people or groups together has broken apart.
  • The break tends to be sharp and significant — not a gradual drifting apart, but a definitive fracture.
  • There is often an identifiable moment or event that caused it.
What Makes a Rupture Different from a Simple "Break"?

This is an important distinction. Not every break is a rupture. The word "rupture" carries specific weight:

Ruptures are usually:

  • Sudden — they happen quickly, not gradually.
  • Forceful — there is pressure, stress, or violence involved.
  • Significant — a rupture tends to matter. It disrupts, damages, or destroys something that was functioning.
  • Visible or felt — the break is noticeable, often dramatic.

You wouldn't say a tiny crack in your coffee mug is a rupture. But you would say a dam wall suffering a catastrophic tear is a rupture. The scale and force of the break is what earns that word.

The word carries a certain weight and gravity. When you read or hear it, it signals that something important has gone wrong — not a minor inconvenience, but a real break in something that mattered. Whether it's a burst blood vessel, a broken alliance, or a fractured friendship, a rupture always suggests that the damage is real, sudden, and consequential.
Putting It All Together — A Summary

A rupture is the sudden, forceful breaking or bursting of something — a physical object, a bodily tissue, or an abstract bond like a relationship or agreement. The thing that ruptures was previously whole and holding together; after the rupture, it is torn, broken, or split apart, often causing serious harm or disruption. Whether you're talking about a burst pipe, a torn tendon, or a collapsed friendship — a rupture always means: something that should have stayed whole didn't.
14019: When something ruptures, it breaks open suddenly and forcefully — usually because internal pressure has built up to a point where the object can no longer hold itself together, or because an extreme external force causes it to give way. The moment of rupturing is violent, abrupt, and consequential. It is not a slow crack or a gentle split. It is a decisive failure.

Physically, things that rupture are almost always things that were containing something — liquid, gas, or pressure — or things that were holding two parts of something together. When they rupture, that containment or connection catastrophically fails.

A gas pipeline ruptured during the earthquake. His spleen ruptured on impact. The dam ruptured after days of flooding. The appendix ruptured before the doctors could operate.

In each case, notice that something which was whole and under stress suddenly broke open, releasing or exposing what was inside. The rupturing itself is the moment of violent failure, and its consequences are usually serious.

This is a crucial distinction. "Rupture" is stronger and more dramatic than simply "break." If a cup breaks, it falls and cracks into pieces — that's ordinary damage. But if something ruptures, it implies an internal force, a pressure threshold being crossed, and a violent giving-way. A balloon doesn't just break; it ruptures or bursts. A blood vessel doesn't just break; it ruptures.

"Burst" is actually the closest word in meaning to "rupture," but "rupture" carries a slightly more formal, clinical, and severe tone. You'd hear "burst" in casual speech and "rupture" in medical reports, engineering assessments, and serious journalism. "Rupture" also implies that the thing was meaningful and functional before it failed — the word draws attention to the loss of integrity.

"Rupture" works both ways, and it is important to understand both.

Used intransitively (the subject ruptures on its own, no additional object needed): The pipe ruptured. Her eardrum ruptured during the deep dive. The fuel tank ruptured on contact.

Used transitively (something or someone causes the rupture): The explosion ruptured the fuel tank. The impact ruptured his liver. Pressure from the flood ruptured the levee.

Both uses are correct and common. The choice depends on whether you want to focus on the thing that failed or the force that caused the failure.
The Figurative Meaning — When Abstract Things Rupture

This is where "rupture" becomes truly powerful and widely used. It is regularly applied to things you cannot physically touch — relationships, alliances, trust, diplomacy, peace, and social bonds.

When used figuratively, "rupture" means a serious, sudden breakdown that leaves something profoundly damaged, possibly beyond repair. The betrayal ruptured their friendship. The scandal ruptured diplomatic relations between the two nations. His lie ruptured whatever trust had remained between them. Years of tension finally ruptured the alliance.

The figurative meaning carries all the same weight as the literal one — the idea of something that was once intact and under strain finally giving way in a dramatic, irreversible moment. You are not saying the relationship was merely hurt or damaged; you are saying it broke open in a way that cannot be quietly patched.

Whenever you use "rupture," you are communicating several things at once without spelling them out:

Suddenness. The rupturing happened at a specific, identifiable moment, not gradually over time.

Severity. Whatever ruptured was significantly damaged — not superficially. The consequences matter.

Pressure. There was a build-up — of internal pressure, external force, or accumulated strain — that preceded the rupture. The rupture is the culmination.

Wholeness lost. Before the rupture, the thing was intact and functional. The rupturing marks a clear before and after.

"Rupture" is a moderately formal word. You will encounter it most naturally in medical contexts, engineering and infrastructure reporting, news coverage of political breakdowns, and literary writing. In casual everyday conversation, people tend to say "burst" or "broke" instead. But when you choose the word "rupture," it signals seriousness — you are not being casual or imprecise.
The Image to Lock It In

Picture a fully pressurized water pipe, cold and holding. Pressure keeps building inside it. Then — in one violent instant — it gives way, splitting open, water spraying out under force, the pipe irreparably broken. That moment — the sudden, forceful, pressure-driven giving-way of something that was once whole — is the heart of what "rupture" means. It doesn't matter whether it's a blood vessel, a tendon, a levee, a friendship, or a geopolitical alliance. If it ruptured, something that was intact and under strain has violently broken apart, and nothing is the same afterward.
